en: Annotated Edition of the *Buddhabhāṣita-poṣadha-sūtra* Translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Qian of the Wu [Dynasty] Annotated by the Śrāmaṇera Zhixu of the Ming [Dynasty]
I shall now explain the two versions of the profound meaning (*xuányì*) of this sutra: first, that which follows the text; second, that which transcends the sections.

Regarding the first, that which follows the text, it is roughly as set forth in the *Púsà jì yìshū* (Commentary on the Meaning of the Bodhisattva Precepts), where three levels of profound meaning are presented: first, the explanation of names (*shìmíng*); second, the determination of essence (*chūtǐ*);
and third, the analytical discussion (*liàojiǎn*). As for the explanation of names: this refers to the disciples of the two lay assemblies during the third month of the year.
The six items received are called the Eight Precepts of the Fast (aṣṭāṅga-śīla-upavāsa); alternatively, they may be expanded into nine, but here they are condensed into eight.
This is because abstaining from killing and so forth are termed "precepts" (śīla), while abstaining from eating at improper times is termed the "fast" (upavāsa).

Yet, when the title refers to it solely as the "fast," it uses a specific term to encompass the general, employing the essence to designate the constituent parts. Furthermore, the fast is also called a precept, for it was established by the Buddha; thus, it is a precept.
It is also called "fasting" (*upavāsa*) because it brings the three karmas into alignment: when the body is aligned, there is no filth; when speech is aligned, there are no transgressions;

when the mind is aligned, there are no afflictions or outflows (*āsrava*). Thus, for one day and one night, by maintaining a sincere resolve, one purifies the will internally through the five reflections and restrains the body and speech externally through the eight limbs. When these three paths of karma are purified, one emerges [from the fast].
The worldly norm is the meaning of that which is produced through causes and conditions.

Not perceiving within an "I" who receives the precepts, not perceiving without a person who bestows the Dharma, and not apprehending in between the Dharma that is received—yet practicing single-mindedly without slackening, without retreating, and without hesitation—this is precisely the meaning of emptiness. Relying upon this is the true fast.
The Dharma thus possesses ten realms with differing causes and effects, namely: either faith or lack of faith; acceptance or non-acceptance; upholding or disparaging;
upholding while attached to marks or upholding while detached from marks; practicing solely for oneself or for the sake of sentient beings;
being incomplete or bringing [practice] to completion. This is precisely the meaning of the provisional. Day One.

The nature of the one-night fast is beyond measure; its eight branches and five recollections are the Dharma-realm itself. As both the sustainer and the sustained, whether in terms of phenomena or principle, they are inherently free from dependence.
To raise one is to encompass all; therefore, it is said that the word *zhāi* (fast) signifies "to equalize" (*qí*).

Like the ocean seal manifesting clearly, it extends horizontally and exhausts the vertical, such that there is not a single dharma that is not fully provided for; this is what is called [the Great Fast].

To align with this is the meaning of "the Middle" (*madhyama*). To facilitate easy understanding, this sequence has been established; once the underlying principle is grasped, one can speak of it as the causal conditions [for practice].

The same applies to emptiness, the Middle, and the provisional (*śūnyatā-madhyamā-prajñapti*). The Buddha’s teachings and the scriptures are fully explained as is customary. Second, regarding the determination of its essence (*svabhāva*):
the very abstention from eating at improper times constitutes the essence of the *poṣadha*; the remaining branches serve as auxiliary factors that bring it into being.
The primary cause of death is none other than sexual desire, and the most predominant and superior condition for the increase of birth and death is none other than food and drink;
therefore, the Sūtra says that all sentient beings sustain their very lives by depending on sexual desire, and it further states that all sentient beings abide by depending on food.
Thus, those who live as householders have not yet been able to permanently abandon the conditions of domestic affairs, kinship, and possessions.

Because of these accumulations, it is ordained that on the six days of fasting (ṣaḍ-upoṣadha), one should receive these Eight Precepts of the Fast (aṣṭāṅga-śīla) for one day and one night, thereby planting the causes and conditions for eternal deliverance in future lives.
Taking the fast as its essence, this distinguishes it from the five precepts for life which are inferior, and from the ten precepts of a śrāmaṇera which are superior;
based on what is received here, the one-day, one-night precepts and the fast likewise give rise to [merit].

For one day and one night, there is the non-manifesting wholesome form (*avijñapti-śīla*), because from the moment it is undertaken at dawn, it is natural for one to cease evil and practice good, and thus untainted merit (*anāsrava-puṇya*) is produced. Regarding the third point of analysis, there are six types of persons who may receive this fast (*upavāsa*):
namely, bodhisattvas and male or female lay followers (*upāsaka/upāsikā*), provided they have reached the age of three months or six months.

Those who do not receive this fast incur the offense of a transgression against the half or full precepts, as well as those who merely take the Three Refuges, whether male or female lay devotees (*upāsaka* or *upāsikā*), who should receive this fast during the three months of the year on the sixth day of each month to create the causes for transcendence.

Even the eight classes of spirits and deities, as well as animals that understand human speech, may uphold the rites of this fast in the hope of escaping the wheel of suffering. There are nine types of persons [who may do so].
"Receiving [the precepts] without accomplishing the fast" refers to those who have received the Bodhisattva precepts but have violated the root [offenses], as well as bhikṣus,
bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who have already broken the root precepts;
and it also refers to those who have received this one-day and one-night fast method (upavāsa) but have violated the four grave root precepts.
Those who are unable to receive it may instead rely on Mahāyāna repentance to obtain a vision of auspicious signs, after which they may continue to receive it as before.
To receive this *upavāsa* dharma, one must have at least one ordained person serve as a witness;

regardless of whether they belong to the Great or Small Vehicle or to any of the five assemblies (*pañca-saṃgha*), provided they never eat at improper times for the rest of their lives, they may serve as a teacher even if they reside several *li* away.
Internally, one must resolve that such a person does not exist; rather, one may personally vow to uphold and receive [the precepts] before a sūtra or an image.

Second, regarding the "crossing of the joints," there are five further layers: taking the single dharma as the name, the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) as the essence (*tattva*), supramundane right causes as the school (*mūla*), birth in heaven and *nirvāṇa* as the function (*prayojana*), and placing poison in milk as the teaching aspect (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*). This is the first dharma.

That which is termed "name" is what is called *zhāi* (fasting/abstinence). *Zhāi* carries the meaning of "equalizing. Because the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-differentiated in their threefold nature, it is called "equalizing.

When one is deluded regarding this single mind, by equalizing with all Buddhas above, one refrains from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, drinking alcohol, and indulging in the five sensory objects (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), yet remains unaware of shame and remorse; when one is deluded regarding this single mind, by equalizing with all conscious beings below, one likewise acts in such a manner.

Within the Dharma of equality, one gives rise to the perception of self and other, conceives attachment and views, clings to a self, harms others, and becomes deluded regarding this single mind, which is the entirety of the Middle Way.
Consequently, one either commits the offense of killing in fact or kills in principle; commits the offense of stealing in fact or steals in principle;
and likewise for sexual misconduct, lying, food and drink, flowers, incense, music, and fine seats—there is nothing that does not follow suit, resulting in the ten [unwholesome paths].

Now, having thoroughly understood the distinctions of the realms, causes, and effects, and realizing that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is undefiled and free from the faults of the five desires, one practices in accordance with the *śīla-pāramitā*.
Whether in terms of phenomena or principles, being fully endowed with purity, one thereby brings the actions of body, speech, and mind into accord with the Middle Way;
above, they harmonize with the compassionate power of all Buddhas, and below, they accord with the sorrow for sentient beings.
Looking up to its name, it is called the *Caiwen* (Text on Fasting). The text states:

"To maintain the mind as that of a true person (*zhēnrén*) for the duration of one day and one night, even unto the purity of the precepts—this is what is meant by practicing with a single mind. Next, regarding taking the *dharmatā* (true reality) as its essence:

originally, this sutra stems from the *Āgamas* and should accord with the three seals [of the Dharma]. If it lacked these three seals, it would become no more than "herding cattle" [a mere worldly practice].
Furthermore, the Niganthas’ fasting ritual consists of three seals that constitute the Buddha-dharma’s fasting ritual;

however, since one now upholds the *Lotus Sūtra* and its revealed supreme teaching, one must know that these three seals are in reality but a single seal, because there is no duality between the essence of birth-and-death and nirvāṇa.

If one were to explain this extensively by traversing all dharmas, the precept against killing—protecting and being mindful of all beings—is essentially the unconditioned great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*).
The precept of non-stealing, characterized by loving-kindness (*maitrī*), has as its essence great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) that is without objective conditions (*anālambana*).

The precept of celibacy, characterized by purity and freedom from defilement, has as its essence the stainless Brahma-conduct (*vimala-brahmacarya*). The precept of refraining from false speech, characterized by uprightness and sincerity, has as its essence suchness (*tathatā*).

The precept of abstaining from intoxicants, characterized by a mind free from negligence, has as its essence numinous wisdom (*jñāna*). The precept of not being attached to incense and flowers is free from...
The precept of not adorning the body is the pure adornment; the precept of abstaining from song and dance is the tranquility of the body’s stillness and the cessation of all clamor and agitation;
the precept of not being fond of high beds is the seat of the emptiness of all dharmas that abandons the mind of arrogance;

and the precept of not eating at improper times is the ultimate *sarvajñā* (all-knowing wisdom), wherein there is no further need beyond the Middle Way—this is what it means to be one who recollects the Buddha.
The essence of mindfulness of the Dharma is the Dharmakāya; the essence of mindfulness of the Saṃgha is liberation;

the essence of mindfulness of the precepts is the three clusters (triskandha), which is also the three virtues (triguṇa); the essence of mindfulness of the devas is the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya).
For one day and night, their essence spans from antiquity to the present. Since all such things are merely different names for the true mark (lakṣaṇa), they are directly [identical].
The true reality (*dharmatā*) is the primary essence. Next, regarding the "principle" (*zong*) of the supramundane correct cause: there are three types of worlds—first, the world of common dwelling;
second, the world of skillful means; and third, the world of true retribution. To maintain the fast of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is to produce the correct cause for the world of common dwelling;

to maintain the fast of the provisional (*upāya*) is to produce the correct cause for the world of skillful means; and to maintain the fast of the Middle Way (*madhyamā*) is [to produce the cause for the world of true retribution].
This is the true cause for producing the retribution of the fruit. Next, regarding "producing birth in heaven and *nirvāṇa* as its function":

birth in heaven is the proximate fruit, while *nirvāṇa* is the remote fruit. Furthermore, there are the heavens of karmic retribution, the heavens of purity, and the heavens of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*);
those who maintain this fast shall all attain birth therein. There are also the *nirvāṇa* of perfect purity, the *nirvāṇa* of the means of purity, and the *nirvāṇa* of intrinsic purity.

Those who maintain this *naiḥsargika-śīla* (the fast of Nirvana) will ultimately all attain it. Next, as for placing poison within milk and curd as a pedagogical device, it was as when [the Buddha] first explained the Dharma of the five precepts to Trapusa and Bhallika;
many attained the realization of the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena) through profound mystery. This is not the case with the barbarians (*hu*).
How much more so for practitioners today who uphold the intent of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* while receiving this fast—how could they not attain [realization] during the fast?
That those within possess the Buddha-nature and abide in the secret treasury can be known; there is no need for extensive explanation.
Entering into the text, it is divided into three parts: first, the introductory section (nidāna); second, the main body of the teaching (śarīra); and third, the dissemination section (pariṇāmana).
△ First, the introductory section has two parts: first, the testimony of faith; second, the occasion for the teaching. Now, the first:
"Thus have I heard at one time the Buddha was staying in the palace of the Prime Minister’s residence to the east of Śrāvastī."
The testimony of faith consists of five phrases: first, the hearing; second, the essence of the Dharma; third, the time; fourth, the teacher; and fifth, the location.
Briefly stated, these exclude the "those who heard together. Regarding the ritual for receiving the fast (upavāsa), one may either go to a monastery or invite a master to one's own home;
here, it is the reception at home.
△ 2. The Arising of the Resolve.

The mother of the Prime Minister, named Viśākhā, rose early in the morning, bathed, and donned colorful garments. Accompanied by her sons and daughters-in-law, she went forth, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
The Buddha asked Viśākhā, “Why have you bathed so early? She replied, “I wish to [bathe] with my daughters-in-law.”
Both [the laity] should receive the precepts of the fast.

The two assemblies of householders should both receive the fast; now, as the Chancellor’s mother is the initiator, it is especially difficult for a woman, who is constantly occupied with domestic affairs, to uphold them.
To cite what is difficult serves to manifest what is easy. Furthermore, the upāsakas receive the fast.
For laywomen (*upāsikā*), it is convenient to receive the fast (*poṣadha*) at a monastery; for those in Vaiśālī, it is convenient to do so at home.

Since the "colored robes" (*cāiyi*) are the ordinary garments worn at home, and as they do not interfere with the eight precepts (*aṣṭāṅga*), there is no specific rule requiring them to be dyed a monastic color (*kāṣāya*).
However, if one who has already received the Bodhisattva Upāsaka precepts possesses the three seamless robes (*tricīvara*), they should obtain [the fast] on the day of the *poṣadha*.

[This section] is recorded here. △ Second, the Main Body of the Teaching (Zhengzongfen), which has two parts: first, striking the responsive capacity; second, the formal instruction. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the Buddha’s counter-interrogation;
second, the request from those present. Herein begins the first.
The Buddha said, "There are three classes of those who observe the fast (*upoṣadha*);

which class of fast do you prefer? 'Class' (*pe*) means category. Although the dharma of the fast is the same, it results in three distinct types solely due to differences in the minds that uphold and receive it;

one must carefully examine and choose what one prefers. If one’s aspiration and inclination are toward the True Dharma, it is correct; if one’s aspiration and inclination are toward the Great [Vehicle], it is likewise [correct]."
The merit of this clarity is indeed infinite.
△ Second, the request from the audience:
Vimalakīrti knelt long and said, "I wish to hear what is meant by the three fasts."
△ Second, the correct exposition [of the three types of observances]. First, listing their names; second, explaining each individually.
Now, for the first: The Buddha said: "First is the cowherd’s observance; second is the Nirgrantha’s observance; third is the Buddhist observance."

Relying on craving is like being a cowherd; relying on views is like being a Nirgrantha. To sever craving and views and cultivate the Eightfold Path and the Five Mindfulnesses is called the Buddha-dharma.
"Nirgrantha" (尼犍) is a name for a non-Buddhist outsider, translated here as "one who has abandoned bonds."

△ Second, the explanation, which has two parts: first, the metaphor; second, the application. Now, the first:
It is like a cowherd who seeks out fine water and grass to drink and feed his cattle; at evening, returning home, he reflects on which pasture was most abundant.
"Even if one must wait until dawn to go again,
it is like this: though one may receive the fast according to the Buddha-dharma on this day, if one does not maintain the eight branches of the mind nor practice the five recollections,
yet instead harbors thoughts of the five desires for the next day, it is like a cowherd who anticipates the water and grass for tomorrow."
Applying this analogy by extension, those who uphold the Buddha’s precepts in this life and aspire for the joy of humans and devas in the future are all like cowherds.
△ Second, the combination.
If members of a clan, whether men or women, having received the precepts of fasting, set their minds upon the benefits and desires of household life,
or think of fine food and drink to nourish and sustain the body, they are like those cowherds.

Although they receive the precepts and vows, they do not contemplate the eightfold path of renunciation or the fivefold mindfulness; because they have fallen into the net of craving, they are like cowherds.
△ Third, the conclusion.
One cannot obtain great merit without great illumination.
Indeed, the method of fasting and precept-keeping for one day and one night is fundamentally the true cause for transcending the world;
yet, if the mind aspires to the five desires and entangles itself in the net of craving—just as if one were to trade a mani jewel for a single garment or a single meal—it is therefore not so.
The attainment of supramundane great merit arises from the light of supramundane great wisdom;
since the aspirations of the mind are thus base and inferior, the concluding judgment states that it is not the Great Illumination (Mahāprajñā).
△ Second, the explanation of the *Nirgrantha* fast, in three parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation; third, the conclusion. Now, the first: "The *Nirgrantha* fast.
△ Second, the explanation, which has two parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the pointing out of errors. Now, the first.
On the fifteenth day of the month during the time of the fast, one prostrates on the ground to receive the precepts of fasting and pays homage to the deities within ten *yojanas*, saying:
"Today I observe the fast and dare not commit evil. I do not claim to have a home; there is no kinship between 'self' and 'other.
Wife, children, servants, and slaves are not mine, and I am not their master."
"Yojana" is translated as "xiang" (direction/extent); it is also called "youxun," which is forty *li*.
"Facing the various deities" means that one does not know how to take refuge in the Triple Gem.
Nevertheless, although [the text] does not list all eight branches in detail, its general meaning is similar to the Buddha's precepts; therefore, below, its faults will be correctly pointed out.
△ Second, the refutation of errors:

However, in their studies, they value the literary form while disparaging the substance; lacking a correct mind that reaches the ultimate goal, their mutual naming of appearances has become like a mere historical anecdote.
Since they do not claim to have a family and have no kinship with others, how are they any different from the Buddha-dharma?

That they are merely called followers of the Nirgrantha fast is not only because they do not know where to take refuge in the Triple Gem, but because their learning prizes outward form while disparaging inner substance, and they lack a correct mind.
To prize outward form means to apply elaborate ornamentation to the exterior in order to seek pleasure.
Those of base nature, whose ears and eyes are dull, do not understand true cultivation or actual realization—returning to the root and reverting to the source.
To simply contemplate *tathatā* (Suchness) is called "rectifying the mind"; yet, as long as one is not liberated from the net of views, it is said that one lacks a rectified mind.

Since the delusions of view remain entangled and the habitual tendencies of craving persist, by the following day things are just as they were before. This is why non-Buddhists value external forms and texts.
That those of base nature lack a correct mind is truly because they do not know the world-transcending Dharma-gate of the Three Jewels.
Although they now take refuge in the Three Jewels, they do not contemplate the essential means of liberation; instead, they continue to value literary form while disparaging substance.

One should know that they are the same as the non-Buddhist Nirgranthas; if one were to divide them into categories, there would be four permutations. The first is: not taking refuge in the Three Jewels, yet valuing...
First, those who disparage the essential nature [of the Dharma] and take the Nirgranthas as their ultimate refuge;

second, those who value straightforwardness and the pursuit of righteousness, who are the Confucian masters of this land, yet do not take refuge in the Triple Gem solely because they have not encountered the Dharma-gate of the Triple Gem, and thus have no one to rely upon;

and third, those who possess a straightforward and upright mind but, upon encountering the Triple Gem, fail to take refuge in it. As for the third category, those who turn toward and take refuge in the Triple Gem...

Fourth, those whose minds are upright and correct are true disciples of the Buddha. Although they take refuge in the Triple Gem, if they value literary form while disparaging essential substance, they are non-Buddhists in affiliation with the Buddha-dharma.

By extension, those who receive the precepts value the outward manifestation of the name of "upholding the Vinaya," yet their nature and prohibitions regarding various karmas are not necessarily subtle and pure. Likewise, those who expound the teachings value the outward manifestation of being a "propagator."
Those who cultivate and realize the Dharma may not necessarily have a thorough and clear understanding of its essential path;

those who practice *chan* (meditation) may value the reputation of manifesting spiritual efficacy while failing to exhaustively investigate the source or reach the ultimate bottom of their own fundamental matter;

and those who perform repentance rituals may value the reputation of vocal intonation and formal ceremony while lacking deep familiarity with or actual implementation of the precepts, principles, and contemplations. All such cases are alike.
If one were to discuss the categories of the Nirgranthas based on their teachings, their treatises, their essential nature, and their correct mental state,
then all nine realms would be termed Nirgranthas.
△ Third, the conclusion.
One who observes the fast in such a manner does not attain great merit nor great illumination.

This means that although one may receive the Buddhist fast, if—as in those cases—one values form while disparaging substance and lacks a correct mind, it is like placing *sarpis* (clarified butter) in a vessel of poison;
how could it nourish people? It is neither the merit nor the wisdom of world-transcendence.
△ Second, the extensive explanation of the first [topic], which has three parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation; third, the conclusion. Now, for the first:
"The Buddhist Dharma fast" (buddhadharma-upavāsa).

The Bodhisattva precepts may be received by both groups of the laity; these are called the "Monthly Six Uposatha Days," namely the eighth, fourteenth, fifteenth, twenty-third, twenty-ninth, and thirtieth days of the month.
If the month is short, the twenty-eighth day is taken to complete the count. On these six days, the Four Heavenly Kings and their...
On the days when the Son’s messengers patrol the world, receiving the fast and cultivating merit brings double the benefit compared to other times.
Regarding the "Three Long Fasting Months" of the year, the monthly fasts are somewhat difficult to accommodate, so one may observe them according to one's capacity;

however, the daily fast is easiest and should especially be upheld during the three months of the year—namely, the first, fifth, and ninth months—which are the portions assigned to Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King.
Those in Jambudvīpa should likewise observe the fast and cultivate merit. The eight precepts are fully set forth as listed below;

Someone might raise this objection: "To do good and eliminate evil, one ought to proceed in continuous succession; if [the practice] were merely..."

if one acts wickedly on those remaining days and waits for the celestial deities to conduct their inspection before cultivating goodness, is this not nearly the same as a petty person concealing their evil while putting forth their goodness?
When a gentleman observes such a person, he sees right through them to their very heart and liver. Can one deceive the celestial deities? He replied: "As for those who receive the six..."

the Eightfold Restraints (Bāṣṭha-kuśala-dharma) are added on six specific days. This is like the feudal lords of the various states:

how could they ever fail to cultivate their governance and spread their virtue in their ordinary times? And how could the scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants ever fail to be diligent in their respective duties and vocations in their ordinary times? It is only when...
During the periods of imperial tours of inspection and provincial examinations, one must likewise redouble one's solemnity and adornment;

for this reason, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* establishes the precept against disrespecting auspicious times, and the *Sūtra on the Birth of Goodness* also ordains that failing to observe the six fast days constitutes a transgression of the "intentional" grade.
This serves as a superior merit for Bodhisattvas and acts as a cause for the supramundane for lay practitioners.

At the very least, for those multitudes of sentient beings burdened by many transgressions, even if they cannot cultivate goodness in a continuous stream, one should cause them to temporarily distance themselves from evil karma;
if they are gradually tamed until sprouts of virtue begin to grow, who knows that these oxen and sheep, if not left to roam, might not eventually flourish as fine timber upon the mountain?
As Confucius said: "If there were someone who could apply their strength for even a single day..."
"Regarding benevolence, I have never seen one who lacked the strength [to achieve it]. It is further said:

"If for a single day one can overcome the self and return to ritual propriety (*li*), the whole world will turn to benevolence; if one observes fasting and purification for a single day, the result is likewise.

Even if those of superior capacity are few, to arrive at this state once every month or once every day is still far superior to those who, like the dawn, perish without returning. Thus we know the Tathāgata...
Establishing the Dharma to universally benefit those of the three faculties: some may rest after not long; some may be repeatedly exhorted yet remain without fault;
some may be granted advancement but not permitted to retreat; and some may be granted purity but not guaranteed their past status. It depends entirely upon how the recipient examines themselves.

△ Second, the explanation of the characteristics of the precepts, in eight parts. First, the precept against killing, up to the eighth, the precept against eating at improper times. Regarding the first precept against killing:
for the duration of one full day and night, one maintains the mind like that of a true person (*satpuruṣa*), harboring no intent to kill and maintaining thoughts of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

Sentient beings must not harm or injure even the crawling and wriggling creatures; one must not add the blade of a knife to kill them, but should instead desire their benefit and peace, refraining from killing once more, practicing the pure precepts with a single-minded focus.
To explain the characteristics of these precepts, each is treated according to three intentions: first, the causal conditions; second, the application of the teachings;
and third, the contemplation of the mind. Regarding the explanation of the causal conditions: now, the habitual natures of sentient beings each have their own preferences.

For those who prefer long durations, one speaks of long durations—whether for the remainder of one’s life or until the end of the future. For those who prefer short durations, one speaks of short durations—whether for a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) or so forth.
Regarding the periods of one thought-moment, one day, seven days, one year, and so forth—what is now said to be "the completion of one full day and night" is spoken according to one's inclination.
Although the eightfold pure precepts are very easy [to undertake], they are also very difficult [to maintain];
thus, completing them for a full day and night is difficult yet easy, whereas failing to complete even half a day or half a night is easy yet difficult.
Therefore, establishing a fixed measure of one day and one night—neither decreasing nor increasing—so that people may believe and accept it with joy, is the *loka-siddhānta*.
That wholesome dharmas are easily accomplished so that a virtuous mind necessarily arises is the *pudgala-siddhānta*.
That there are established limits which no one dares to violate, so that evil intentions are necessarily extinguished, is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*.
This is the *yathā-siddhānta* (the standpoint of therapeutic treatment). Nirvāṇa is called "day" and saṃsāra is called "night. When nirvāṇa is exhausted, saṃsāra is exhausted;
when saṃsāra is exhausted, nirvāṇa is exhausted. When both day and night are exhausted, neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa can be apprehended.
Thus, one cuts off the three periods of time in a single sitting and enters the principle suddenly and clearly—this is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the standpoint of ultimate truth).

To hold the mind as that of a "True Person" (*satpuruṣa*): *Arhat* is translated as "Unattached," also as "Non-arising," also as "Worthy of Offerings" (*arhat*), and also as "True Person. Here, it refers to the supramundane fruit of sainthood;
to hold the mind as such means to be like a sage in all that one hears in the world, and to accomplish wholesome dharmas just as a sage does.

To benefit others as a sage by refraining from all evils is the benefit of counteraction; to be like a true person (*satpuruṣa*), like the One, and like that which is non-dual is the benefit of entering into principle.
One who possesses no intent to kill is like a true person who has eternally severed the habit of killing—this is the general indication.
To regard sentient beings with compassion is the specific clarification of practicing goodness, wherein one must not commit harm or injury.
This clearly distinguishes the cessation of evil thoughts and the cultivation of wholesome ones; it clarifies that one should desire benefit and peace, and that one must cease from killing.
This cessation of evil and cultivation of goodness—these two types of virtue—are called the pure precepts of all Buddhas.
Because they are now practiced with a single mind, this is termed "upholding the mind like a true person. Next, regarding the explanation according to the teachings (*yōkyō shaku*), at this time...
Since there are no real dharmas, they are provisionally established based on the states of form and mind; thus, there arise the distinctions of days, months, years, and kalpas.

The sun rising is called day, and the sun setting is called night—this is the intent of the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings (Zangjiao) regarding the absence of self and what belongs to a self (*ātman* and *ātmīya*).

That the sun has neither rising nor setting and that the nature of day and night is empty—this is the intent of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao). Since time is already empty in its nature, it can be extended for one [kalpa].

To take a single day as an eternal kalpa, or to shorten an eternal kalpa into a single day, is the intended meaning of the distinct teachings that cause all sentient beings to have their own individual cognitions and visions.
The ten periods of time—past, present, and future—beginning and ending never depart from the present thought-moment;
the nature of a single kṣaṇa is itself the nature that spans from antiquity to the present. One does not see any dharma that exists outside of this single day.
That which is beyond night is called the exhaustion [of the cycle] within one full day and night; this is the intent of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

To sever and exhaust *dṛṣṭi-āsrava* (views) and *bhāva-āsrava* (afflictions) is to be called a "True Person" (*satpuruṣa*); not killing based on sentient beings constitutes "compassion for sentient beings" (*sattvālambana-maitrī*), which is the intent of the Tripitaka Teaching (*zangjiao*).
Views and afflictions are like empty space and cannot be attained; to be called a "True Person" and not kill based on dharmas constitutes "compassion for dharmas" (*dharmālambana-maitrī*).
The name "Pure Precepts" (śīla-viśuddhi) refers to the general meaning of the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-yāna*): to exhaustively sever the three delusions is called being a "True Person.

Not taking life based on conditions of sentient beings, not taking life based on conditions of dharmas, and not clinging to conditions of self—gradually accomplishing these three forms of compassion is the specific meaning of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*).
The nature of the three delusions is itself the substance of the three *prajñās*; when delusions are transformed into wisdom, it is called "True."

When a person does not move from their Buddha-nature, they accomplish unconditional compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*); this is called the "Pure Precepts," which is the intent of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*).

Regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind (*citta-vipaśyanā*): first, one contemplates the causes and conditions of the mind. Whether time is long or short, it is entirely nothing but the mind.

If one says that the mind is long, then even a short duration is long; it is like the fact that while yellow millet has not yet ripened, [the time] has already passed—this is called the deficiency of the mind. If one says that the mind is... [it is likewise].
If short, then long; even a long duration is short, like an axe-handle already rotted away before a single game of go has ended.
To clearly understand that length and brevity are solely one's own mind, one can then establish length and brevity according to one's will. This is the world of contemplating the mind;

because one realizes that length is not inherently long, one practices the various *pāramitās* throughout immeasurable eons without giving rise to weariness or indolence. This is the contemplation of the mind.
Because people perceive what is short as not being short, they commit sinful transgressions in a single instant and fall into the Avīci Hell; thus, they dare not be negligent.
This is the contemplation of the mind as an antidote. Both long and short are the Dharma-realm, wherein there is no further long or short to be discussed.
To exhaust a single day and night is to exhaust the ultimate limit of birth-and-death and nirvāṇa; this is the primary meaning of the contemplation of the mind.

Contemplating that the mind is originally capable of being that of a True Person, and generating the aspiration accordingly, is the benefit of joy, which further accomplishes the seeds of the three wholesome karmas;

this is like a sage and constitutes the benefit of producing the wholesome. Contemplating that the mind remains far removed from defilements and does not oppose the sages is the benefit of extinguishing evil.
Contemplating that the mind accomplishes the Path of the Sages, yet there is in reality no Path of the Sages to be attained, is the entry into principle.

Next, regarding the contemplation of the mind according to the *yiào* (teaching) classification: when contemplating that the mind is devoid of self and what belongs to a self (*ātman* and *ātmīya*), time and eons are likewise so;
thus, craving and views are severed. This is the intent of the *zhēnrén* (True Person) *zàngjiào* (Tripitaka Teaching).

When contemplating that the nature of the mind is like empty space and cannot be apprehended, time, eons, craving, and views are all identical to empty space. This is the intent of the *zhēnrén* *tōngjiào* (Common Teaching). [Contemplating] the mind...

The provisional designations of the distinctions between immeasurable eons are likewise immeasurable; the wisdom, abandonment, and realization attained are likewise immeasurable—this is according to the intent of the Distinct Teaching (Bie-jiao) for True Persons.

When observing that the mind, being absolute and without dependence, is in its essence the Dharma-realm, such that time, eons, afflictions, and wisdom are all none other than the Dharma-realm—this is according to the intent of the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao) for True Persons. One observes that a single thought-moment is replete [with all phenomena].
Since the provisional and ultimate aspects of all dharmas— whether partial or complete— are neither deficient nor redundant,
how could one not explain the true meaning of these eight branches and five recollections by means of contemplative understanding?
△ Second, the Precept Against Stealing.
Regarding the second precept: for the duration of one day and night, maintain the mind as that of a true person;
free from thoughts of greed or grasping, one should contemplate giving with joy, giving with one's own hands, giving with purity, giving with reverence, and giving without expectation.
One should cast away thoughts of stinginess and greed, practicing this pure precept with a single-minded focus.
The three explanations above can be understood as previously set forth; all subsequent sections follow this pattern. Regarding the intention of non-greed and non-grasping:

first, the virtues of cessation are clarified through mindfulness of giving and so forth; next, the virtues of cultivation are clarified through joy and so forth. These four phrases encompass the four *siddhāntas* (purposes):

"joy" corresponds to the worldly purpose (*loka-siddhānta*), as it involves using one's own hands to generate goodness for others; "purity" corresponds to the remedial purpose (*pratipakṣa-siddhānta*), as it entails distancing oneself from defilements.

Because it is unwholesome, reverence is the contemplation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) that living beings are like Buddhas. Next, the phrase "not hoping" refers to the practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding) as discussed in the treatise;
it means being without expectation for either present or future rewards. The four phrases on "rejoicing" serve to eliminate the mind of stinginess.

The phrase "not hoping to give" eliminates the mind of greed—namely, stinginess regarding wealth and stinginess regarding the Dharma, as well as craving for existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*) and craving for emptiness (*śūnyatā-tṛṣṇā*).
To completely eliminate greed for the two extremes, greed for the middle way, and so forth—this is called the pure precept of all Buddhas.
△ Third, the precept against sexual misconduct.
Regarding this third precept: for one day and one night, one maintains the mind like that of a true person, free from lustful intent and without thoughts of the chamber.
Cultivating the holy life (*brahmacarya*) means not engaging in perverse desires and having no mind that covets form; one practices with a single-mindedness according to pure precepts.

The two phrases regarding "the absence of lustful intent" first clarify the cultivation of wholesome conduct through cessation (*śamatha*), followed by the cultivation of wholesome conduct through application (*samādāna*).

The holy life refers to the four dhyānas and the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*). The two phrases regarding "not engaging in perverse desires" reiterate the wholesome conduct of cessation; "lust" (*maithuna*) is defined as craving (*rāga*).

The defilement of passion, the passion of men and women, the passion for the flavor of dhyāna, the passion for the partial truth, the passion for illusory existence, and the passion for the "but-middle" (but-madhyamaka)—all such inclinations are entirely without name;

they are without the inclination toward lust. Not to think of the sexual acts of the human realm, nor the sexual acts of the form and formless realms, nor the remaining types of sexual acts, nor the sexual acts that are karmic retribution—to not think of these at all is called "not thinking of sexual acts. To know that dhyāna is itself emptiness is...

The provisional is itself the middle; the accomplishment of the loving-kindness that takes beings as its object, phenomena as its object, or has no object, is called the cultivation of the mind of pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
Taking phenomena externally is all termed perverse desire. The nine realms of wholesome, unwholesome, outflowing, and non-outflowing phenomena are all termed form (*rūpa*).
Non-attachment toward all of these is called the pure precept (*viśuddha-śīla*).
△ The Fourth Precept on False Speech.
Regarding the fourth precept: for one day and one night, maintain the mind as that of a true person, free from the intent to speak falsely.

One should contemplate with sincerity, remain stable, and speak slowly; without practicing hypocrisy or deception, let the mind and speech correspond, observing this pure precept with single-mindedness.
Practice.

With the intention of no false speech, one generally marks the permanent abandonment of the four faults; with sincere thought, one is free from the transgression of claiming to have attained what one has not;
with mental stability, one avoids frivolous chatter; with measured speech, one avoids harsh words; and one does not engage in hypocrisy or deception.

That is to say, refraining from divisive speech with mind and mouth in accord, and refraining from false speech—both of these contain the dual sense of the virtues of restraint (*saṃvara*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*), which can be understood through reflection.
△ Fifth: The Precept Against Drinking Alcohol.
The fifth precept is to maintain the mind as that of a true person for one day and one night:

not drinking alcohol, not becoming intoxicated, not falling into confusion, not losing one's resolve, and removing thoughts of negligence; practicing this with a single-minded focus as a pure precept.
The phrase "not drinking alcohol" serves as a general heading for the avoidance of all faults. Intoxication and delusion are both inevitable consequences of drinking;

the dissipation of the will is a category of behavior akin to drinking. To exhaustively apply this principle to its ultimate extent, one must be free from dissipation regarding all three realms and six sense objects before it can truly be called the pure precept.
△ Sixth: The Precept Against Perfumes, Flowers, Song, and Dance.
Regarding the sixth precept: for one day and one night, maintain the mind as that of a true person;

seek no comfort, do not attach to perfumes or flowers, do not apply unguents or powders, and do not engage in song, dance, or musical entertainment. Practice this with a single-minded focus, as if observing the pure precepts.
Forms, sounds, fragrances, tangibles, and other sensory objects are the domains where the six faculties (ṣaḍindriya) find their rest;
now, having closed these six faculties and focused exclusively on seeking the essential path of deliverance, one does not cling to them, does not transmit them, and does not engage in them.

By analogy, Kāśyapa’s dancing upon hearing the lute was likewise due to the fact that his delusions of thought regarding the realms had not yet been eliminated; thus, it follows that the fragrances, flowers, songs, and dances of the three lands are all likewise [subject to this].
Not being attached and not acting [for gain] is precisely what is called the pure Buddha-precepts.
△ The seventh precept: the prohibition against high and wide beds.
Regarding this seventh precept, one should maintain the mind as that of a true person for one day and one night, seeking no comfort and not lying down upon fine [beds].
One should discard low beds, straw mats, and bedding for sleep, and instead contemplate the Way of the Sūtras as one would pure precepts, practicing with a single mind.
What is called a "fine bed" is high, broad, and elaborately adorned; yet to indulge in sleep upon it is no different from a minor death. Now, one must discard it.
Sleeping and reclining is itself the goodness of cessation (*śamatha*); contemplating the sutras and the Way is itself the goodness of cultivation (*vipaśyanā*).

By inferring through this analogy, whatever dharma can be relied upon or clung to is termed a "bed" or "reclining. To realize the emptiness of all dharmas and to take non-abiding as one's abiding—this is called the pure precept (*viśuddha-śīla*).
△ The eighth precept: abstaining from eating at improper times.
Regarding the eighth precept, one maintains the mind for one day and one night as a true person who honors the Dharma;
one eats only at the proper time, eating sparingly and moderating the body, and after midday, one does not eat again. One practices this pure precept with a single-minded focus.

This is correctly named the "Example of the Fasting Rite" (zhāi lǜ), which requires three explanations. First, regarding the causes and conditions: the Buddha’s true Dharma-body does not depend on nourishment from food;

however, his response-body (nirmāṇakāya) is like that of humans, demonstrating the need for sustenance through food and drink. When the sun reaches its zenith at midday, he compassionately accepts offerings.

This is the universal practice of all Sugatas of the ten directions and the single path of all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time. It accords with the way of all Buddhas and is something that people delight in hearing.

The "all-encompassing" (sarva) refers to receiving food at the proper time to sustain the body so that one may cultivate the Way; it is for the purpose of ensuring the body is free from the suffering of illness and the mind attains peace and leisure.
The "person-all-encompassing" (pudgala-sarva) refers to abandoning the fault of greedy attachment to the tip of the tongue and the vexation of constant preoccupation with worldly affairs;

by reducing food and tempering the body, the lustful mind gradually thins. The "counteractive all-encompassing" (pratipakṣa-sarva) refers to taking midday as the symbol of the Middle Way, thereby embodying the Middle Way.

Beyond this, there is nothing further required; this is the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*). Regarding the provisional teaching (*neyārtha*), according to the various realms and continents, one follows the human laws:
once the single meal-time line has passed, one does not swallow again—this is the intent of the Tripitaka teachings.

Although time is fundamentally empty and like an illusion, even at midday one should have no attachment to the taste of food; how much less should one greedily seek it after noon? This is the realization of emptiness.

Therefore, the intent of the *Tongjiao* (Common Teaching) is that by not giving rise to a mind of transgression, one relies on the observance of the fast (*upavāsa*) to produce the fruits of the three evil realms;
whereas by maintaining the fast, one produces the fruits of the good destinies and the three vehicles (*triyāna*).

The intent of the *Biejiao* (Distinct Teaching) is to vow that through this fast, one shall benefit oneself and others—seeking the supreme above and transforming those below—to adorn the Middle Way and proceed toward the ultimate fruit. This is the Middle Way.
This is precisely the single cessation and the single activity of the *dharmadhātu*; eating before midday, may all sentient beings of the *dharmadhātu* attain realization of the Middle Way;
not eating after midday, may all sentient beings of the *dharmadhātu* never again be deluded regarding the Middle Way.
To bind one's conditions to the *dharmadhātu* in a single thought-moment of the *dharmadhātu* is the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*paripūrṇa-yāna*). This is contemplation.

The mind, when the sense organs and their objects encounter one another, all possess the quality of "nutriment" (*āhāra*); for example, the eye has sleep as its nutriment, the ear has sound as its nutriment, and so forth.

If one falls into the trap of either over-intellectualizing or suppressing these functions, one becomes ensnared in the net of nihilistic views; yet if one pursues sounds and chases after forms, one again drifts upon the river of craving.
Now, to speak of "timely nutriment" refers merely to that which conditions present sensory data (*pratyakṣa*), while to speak of "meager nutriment" refers to...
Thus, being free from craving and seeking, one neither perpetually opposes the sentiments of sentient beings nor causes others to feel aversion.
To contemplate the mind is to take the Dharma as sustenance to nourish the spirit; to contemplate the mind is to sever unrighteous sustenance for humans;

to contemplate the mind is the application of remedies that accords with the Middle Way; to contemplate the mind is the primary meaning (paramārtha). Within the six sense-objects, there is neither self nor what belongs to a self.

Neither annihilation nor permanence is called the Middle Way; when the mind does not take annihilation or permanence as its object, it is called "not exceeding the Middle"—this is the contemplation of the Tripitaka Teaching.
The nature of the six sense-objects is empty and illusory, being neither existent nor non-existent; this is called the Middle Way;
when the mind does not take the two extremes of existence and non-existence as its object, it is called "not exceeding the Middle"—this is the contemplation of the Shared Teaching. Six.

The six sense objects each mutually give rise to all phenomena, fully constructing the ten realms; yet their nature is not the ten realms, as they transcend the two extremes and are thus called the Middle Way.
When the mind does not grasp at the food of the two truths—birth-and-death and nirvana—it is called "not exceeding the middle.

This is the contemplation of the Separate Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna-śāsana*). The essence of the six sense objects is itself the Dharma-realm, fully possessing the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses; whichever one is raised, it encompasses them all.

All phenomena within a single atom converge upon this atom; this convergence does not exceed it, nor is there even the slightest phenomenon outside of this single atom that can be called "not exceeding. As it is with one atom, so it is with all atoms;
as it is with all atoms, so it is likewise with all minds, all phenomena, and all provisional designations.

This is the contemplation of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), which holds that non-existence is not separate from the substance of reality, and that within this very center no dharma is seen to transcend it;
thus it is called "not exceeding the center. All such contemplations take the practice of not eating at improper times as their objective basis (*shijing*).

If there were no such objective basis, the contemplation of principle would not arise. Therefore, Jingxi said: "The people of the world despise concrete phenomena while wishing to exalt the profound."

As for the principle: through verification, one knows that this contemplation is solitary, empty, and without foundation; since the object of contemplation is deficient, from where could the contemplation itself arise?
Alas, this is something that can indeed be contemplated.
