Part One: Showing the Objects of Mindfulness. Part Two: Clarifying the Benefits of Mindfulness. Now, the first part.

First, one should practice mindfulness of the Buddha: that the Buddha is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the One Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, the Well-Gone, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed Leader, the Trainer of Gods and Humans, and is titled the Buddha.

In this brief exposition on the ten titles within the context of mindfulness, if one understands the merit of these ten titles, one will understand all the lofty and vast merits of the Buddha’s state;
this too must be briefly clarified through three explanations. First, regarding the causal conditions:
just as worldly sages and worthies also possess many honorable titles—such as "clever," "wise," "intelligent," "divine," "holy," "heroic," and "philosophical"—so it is with the Lord of Devas.

The Buddha has a thousand names, established according to his virtues so that the multitude may joyfully hear them; for a full account, see the "Chapter on Names and Epithets" in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Here, I shall briefly cite ten general titles to manifest his possession of all virtues, which constitutes the knowledge of the world (*loka-jñāna*).
If one hears these ten epithets of the Tathāgata and can thereby generate various roots of goodness, both mundane and supramundane, this constitutes the knowledge of others (*pudgala-jñāna*).
The majestic power of the Ten Epithets enables those who hear them to shatter their narrow and inferior minds and to overcome their arrogance;

they come to revere and stand in awe, not daring to harbor evil intentions—this is the "knowledge of the antidotes" (*pratipakṣa-jñāna*). Furthermore, each individual epithet corresponds to its actual meaning;

upon hearing the name, one realizes its significance and no longer seeks the ultimate truth elsewhere—this is the "knowledge of the ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-jñāna*). In the Sanskrit language, *Tathāgata*...
Regarding this translation of "Tathāgata": if it is said that he comes from nowhere and goes nowhere, he is thus named Tathāgata;

this is an explanation based on the *dharmakāya*. If it is said that he has come to attain perfect enlightenment according to the self-nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), this is an explanation based on the *saṃbhogakāya*.
If it is said that he has come by means of the path of suchness to deliver sentient beings, this is an explanation based on the *nirmāṇakāya*.
The Sanskrit term *arhat* is translated here as "Worthy of Offerings" (*yìnggòng*) and also as "Worthy of Truth" (*yìngzhēn*). Now it is translated as "Ultimate Truth" (*zhìzhēn*);

because he serves as a field of merit for the world, he is called "Worthy of Offerings," and because he darkly accords with his own true nature, he is called "Ultimate Truth. Because he darkly accords with truth, he is capable of acting as a refuge for the world.
The Sanskrit term *sammyaksambuddha* is translated as "Perfectly All-Knowing" (*zhèngbiànzhī*); now it is translated as "Equal" (*děng*).

"Perfectly Awakened" (*samyak-saṃbuddha*) signifies the meaning of pervasiveness; "possessing the complete elucidation of the various Dharma-gates" is termed "Equal" (*sama*), which distinguishes him from the two vehicles by his profound realization of non-differentiation.

This distinguishes him from ordinary worldlings and outsiders. Being endowed with the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*), he is the "One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct" (*vidyā-caraṇa-saṃpanna*).
Excellently transcending the three realms of existence, he is called the "Well-Gone One" (*sugata*), the "Father of the World," and also simply "the World-Honored One."
He who understands himself is liberated and is able to liberate the world, just as a wealthy elder emerges from a burning house and is able to lead his children out of that burning house.

One who is in the stage of "one birth remaining" (ekajātipratibaddha) still has a superior rank; one whose position is at the ultimate limit of wondrous enlightenment, beyond which there is nothing higher, is called the Unsurpassed One (Anuttara).
He is the Charioteer of the Sūtra-Dharma and is also called the Tamer of Men (Puruṣadamyasārathi), for he possesses the qualities of a true man.
The Dharma is that which can expound the sūtras and guide sentient beings. Among the six realms, humans and devas are the most excellent;

furthermore, since the noble ones of the Three Vehicles all abide within the human and celestial realms, the Buddha serves as the teacher and model for these humans and devas—thus, the nine realms alike receive his instruction.
Because he has attained self-awakening, awakened others, and perfected his practice of awakening, he is titled "Buddha" (the Awakened One); he is not called "Worldly."
The Venerable One, endowed with the ten titles, is the most honored in the world; this mentions the specific while briefly indicating the general. Next, regarding the teaching:
by realizing the partial truth (*pratyekasatya*) that lacks the characteristics of coming and going, he uses this to deliver sentient beings—this constitutes "Tathāgata" (Thus Come One) and so forth.

By correctly knowing all worldly phenomena and correctly knowing the supramundane *nirvāṇa*, he is the "Samyaksaṃbuddha" (Perfectly Awakened One). Because he possesses complete knowledge, he is the "Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna" (Endowed with Knowledge and Conduct).

Regarding the past, present, and future, he possesses the "feet of clarity and conduct" (*vidyācaraṇa-sampanna*) and has transcended the three realms of existence, thus being called the "Well-Gone One" (*sugata*).

Having liberated himself from the bonds of the six mundane worlds, he is the Father of the World. Standing above those in the four fruits of the path and the *pratyekabuddhas*, he is the Unsurpassed Being (*anuttara-puruṣa*).

He expounds the ninefold, elevenfold, and twelvefold scriptures to elucidate the principle of arising and ceasing, and as a charioteer who tames sentient beings, he is the Charioteer of the Dharma (*dharmasārathi*).

The guide for those living together is the Teacher of Gods and Humans (*śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām*). Having personally awakened to partial truth (*pradeśasatya*), one also awakens others to that same partial truth;

when both forms of awakening are perfected, one is called a Buddha. This is the meaning of the Tripitaka Teaching (*piṭaka-dharma*). Because birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and Nirvana, there is no coming or going.
One realizes this very emptiness and uses it to deliver sentient beings; as this is the true nature of the Tathāgata, which does not differ from the mundane, it is thus equal.
Because the conventional is not different from the ultimate, he is the Perfectly Awakened One (*samyaksambuddha*).

Contemplating that the nature of the past, future, and present is empty, quiescent, and ungraspable, he is the One Endowed with Knowledge and Conduct (*vidyācaraṇasampanna*). Being within the three realms of existence yet unattached to them, he is the Sugata.
Liberating those bound by the six classes of ordinary beings and the two vehicles, he is the Father of the World. Standing above the three vehicles and the nine stages, he is...
The Unsurpassed One preaches the twelve divisions of the sūtras to elucidate the principle of non-arising;

as a charioteer who tames sentient beings, he serves as the Dharma-charioteer and the guide of skillful means for those dwelling together with him, acting as a teacher of gods and humans. His own awakening to reality is itself the awakening of others to reality;
when both types of awakening are fulfilled, he is called a Buddha. This is the meaning of the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-śāsana*), wherein the Middle Way transcends the two truths.
Therefore, by being without coming or going, one realizes the Middle Way; by using this to deliver sentient beings, one becomes equal to the Tathāgatas.

By correctly knowing the two truths and correctly knowing the Middle Truth, one is the Truly and Fully Enlightened One (*samyaksaṃbuddha*). Reaching back to the furthest limit of the past, exhausting the present, and extending to the furthest limit of the future, one sees all and knows all, becoming the One Endowed with Clarity and Conduct (*vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna*). One successively transcends the realms of common residence, the provisional, and the retributive reward.
He who manifests in the three kinds of lands as the Sugata, who liberates the six classes of ordinary beings and those of the three vehicles from their bonds; who acts as the Father of the World;
who dwells above the ten stages and equal enlightenment as the Unsurpassed One; who expounds the twelve divisions of the sūtras to elucidate immeasurable principles;
who tames and guides sentient beings as the Charioteer of the Dharma; and who serves as the leader for those in the lands of Expedient Means, True Reward, and Ultimate Reality—he is the Deva.
The Teacher of Men awakens to the three truths himself and likewise awakens others to the three truths;

when both forms of awakening are perfected, he is called a Buddha—this is the meaning of the Separate Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*). Because the Middle Way pervades all phenomena, there is no coming or going;

by realizing the perfect Middle Way, one delivers sentient beings, which constitutes the Tathāgata’s awakening. The First Noble Truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is identical to the two truths, and this is termed "Equal Awakening" (*samyaksambodhi*).

That which is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is the "Right and Perfect Enlightenment" (samyak-saṃbodhi). Throughout the ten ages, from antiquity to the present, beginning and end never depart from the present moment;
it enters the three periods of time without coming or going. Within the samādhi of the instant (kṣaṇa-lava), it manifests the accomplishment of Bodhi across oceans of kalpas.
Furthermore, within the eight phases [of enlightenment], it fully possesses the eight phases in an inconceivable manner.

The One Perfect in Clarity and Conduct (Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna) possesses three kinds of lands, none of which are not the Land of Quiescent Light (Śāntaprabhāsa). As the Sugata, he liberates the ten realms from suffering and its origin;
as the Father of the World, he stands above the Dharma-body of the forty-one stages as the Unsurpassed One (Anuttara).

He expounds the twelve divisions of scripture to elucidate the principle of non-action (anabhisaṃskāra), and as the Tamer of Beings, he serves as the Charioteer of the Sūtra-Dharma across the four lands.

He who guides as the Teacher of Gods and Humans has personally awakened to the inconceivable—whether it be the single truth, the two truths, the three truths, or the four truths—and likewise awakens others;

because both forms of awakening are perfected, he is named Buddha. This is the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*):

one contemplates this present, single thought-moment of the mind, which does not abide in any location—neither inside, nor outside, nor in between—and is not something that exists as blue or any other color.
Whether yellow, long, short, or other such characteristics, they cannot be found when sought within the past, future, or present; yet this mind arises clearly and vividly, again and again.

This is the Tathāgata. Since this mind has no spatial dimensions or physical marks, it is fundamentally non-existent throughout the past, present, and future, and is thus free from illusion and delusion—this is the Ultimate Truth. This mind universally knows all dharmas, yet there is nothing [it does not know].
One dharma may serve as a metaphor for this mind as *samyaksambuddha* (perfectly awakened one): this mind is without beginning, without end, and without limit.

This mind is the one who possesses clear knowledge and conduct (*vidyācaraṇasampanna*): although it pervades the creation of the ten realms, it follows conditions all day long yet remains forever unchanging;
thus it is the *sugata* (well-gone one). This mind is not bound by the dharmas of the ten realms, yet it is able to give birth [to them].
The dharmas of the ten realms serve as the father of the world; this mind can equalize all dharmas, yet no dharma can equal this mind.
It is the Unsurpassed One. This mind is fully endowed with the path of investigation, analysis, and speech;
it alone understands and instructs the other minds and mental factors, serving as the charioteer of the Dharma-scriptures. This mind can manifest as a deva and can manifest as a human.
This is not something that can be accomplished by gods or humans; rather, one acts as a teacher of gods and humans because this mind is inherently such that its numinous awareness is never obscured.

Because it awakens to both self and others without anything remaining unexhausted, it is called "Buddha. First, one contemplates that this mind is fully endowed with the ten titles, surpassing all Buddhas above;
thus one rejoices in oneself and rejoices in others, which is the benefit for the world. One contemplates that the mind is fully endowed with the ten titles.

The accomplishment of the merit of wholesome roots is the benefit for others; the contemplation of the mind being fully endowed with the Ten Epithets destroys views, craving, ignorance, and nescience, which is the benefit of remediation;

the contemplation of the mind being fully endowed with the Ten Epithets—being complete in all things, ultimate, equal, neither decreasing nor increasing—is the benefit of the primary meaning (*paramārtha*), as defined by causes and conditions.
Regarding the contemplation of the dharmas that arise: this mind possesses the ten titles according to the Tripitaka teaching when viewed through the contemplation of emptiness;

it possesses the ten titles according to the Shared Teaching when viewed through the contemplation of the provisional; it possesses the ten titles according to the Distinct Teaching when viewed through the contemplation of the Middle; and it possesses the ten titles according to the Perfect Teaching when viewed through the contemplation of the Middle.
△ Second, explaining the benefits of mindfulness. Part three: First, the actual explanation; second, illustration by analogy; third, the application of the Dharma. Now, for the first:

This practitioner of mindfulness of the Buddha completely eliminates ignorance, evil intentions, and the habit-energy of anger; a virtuous mind arises spontaneously, and they contemplate with joy the deeds of the Buddha.
Since the Buddha possesses the distinctions of the four teachings, the three bodies, and the ten titles, there are likewise four types of mindfulness:

mindfulness of oneself, mindfulness of others, and mindfulness of both self and others. For a detailed understanding, one should consult the *Great Buddha-Topknot Sūtra* (Śūraṅgama Sūtra), specifically the section on the "Perfect Penetration of Avalokiteśvara" and its commentary (*Wénjù*).
The complete eradication of ignorance, malevolent intent, and the habit-energy of anger constitutes *śamatha* (calm abiding).

When wholesome thoughts arise spontaneously, one contemplates the joy of the Buddha’s deeds; this is precisely practicing goodness. Within the context of practicing the cessation of unwholesome states, I have briefly cited the destruction of the three poisons.
What is called "evil intent" refers to the poison of being defiled by the five desires. These three poisons consist of both the manifest (*sammukhībhūta*) and the latent (*vāsanā*);
when both the manifest and the latent are entirely removed, it is like a single lamp that can dispel the darkness of a thousand-year-old chamber. Thus one should reflect.

The Dharma-gate can eliminate delusion; contemplating the true mark (*dharmatā*) can eliminate evil thoughts; and contemplating the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) can eliminate the habitual tendencies of anger.
To speak exhaustively according to the principle, these correspond respectively: every thought-moment eliminates the three poisons along with their correct habitual tendencies.
Regarding the practice of goodness, one thoroughly understands cause and effect; the Buddha speaks only of the fruit when saying that a virtuous mind arises spontaneously—it is indeed produced.

The mind detached from desire, the supramundane mind, the mind that generates the aspiration to transform those below, the mind that generates the aspiration to seek what is above, and the mind of ultimate, unsurpassed *sarvajñā* (all-knowing wisdom)—these are the activities of the Buddha that one delights in through speech and thought.
The three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*) are the Buddha’s activity; the one hundred and eight samādhis are the Buddha’s activity;
the three knowledges (*tri-jñāna*) and five eyes (*pañca-cakṣus*) are the Buddha’s activity; and great kindness, great compassion, and great joy [are likewise].
Great equanimity is the Buddha-work; abiding in suchness is the Buddha-work; flowing in harmony with the nine realms is the Buddha-work;

inducing and transforming all beings is the Buddha-work; relying on the treasury of teachings to contemplate one's own Buddha, to contemplate the Buddha of others, and to contemplate the Buddhas of both self and others—thereby eliminating the three poisons and residual habits of the realm of cohabitation, giving rise to the mind of renunciation and supramundane thought, and delighting in the treasury of teachings—is the Buddha-work.

The various wondrous activities of the fruit-Buddha rely on the three types of mindfulness of the Buddha according to the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*), which eliminate the three poisons of the *tongju* (co-resident) and *fangbian* (provisional) lands,

bring about the cessation of their residual habits (*xi*), and give rise to the supramundane mind and the thought of downward transformation. These wondrous activities rely on the three types of mindfulness of the Buddha according to the Distinct Teaching (*bhedaka-śāsana*),

which eliminate the three poisons and both the active and residual habits (*zheng-xi*) of the *tongju*, *fangbian*, and *shibao* (true retribution) lands, and give rise to the downward transformation.

Regarding the aspiration for the supreme mind that delights in the wondrous deeds of the distinct Buddhas based on the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), one practices the three types of mindfulness of the Buddha to eliminate the three poisons and residual habits within the four lands, thereby giving rise to the mind that seeks the ultimate, unsurpassed seed-wisdom (*anuttara-jñāna*). Question:

Why are there still the three poisons and residual habits in the Land of Quiescent Light (*jiguang*)? Answer: This refers to the Land of Quiescent Light from the perspective of partial realization (*fenzheng*). This...
The text also fully embodies the intent of the four *siddhāntas*: mindfulness of the Buddha is the world-view; the removal of the three poisons is the remedial view;
the arising of wholesome thoughts is the view for persons; and the activity of the Buddha is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
△ Second, the illustration by analogy:
For example, just as head-dirt and turbidity are removed by using sesame oil and cleansing powder (*snāna-kaṣāya*),
the sesame oil and cleansing powder that remove filth serve as a metaphor for the mindfulness and wisdom of the four teachings, all of which are instruments for eliminating delusions.

Based upon the Three Treasures of Essential Unity, there exists the Three Treasures of Sustained Maintenance; among these Three Treasures, the Buddha Treasure is the most honored, which may be likened to the head.
One should know that the Buddha Treasure of sustained maintenance is precisely the Buddha Treasure of one's own essential nature.
Once defilements are removed, the head becomes pure; through the merit of nien-fo (buddha-recollection), the Buddha-nature is manifested.
△ Third, the Convergence of the Three Dharmas.
Those who observe the fast while reciting the Buddha’s name attain such purity that all who see them cannot help but believe and admire it.
Because they receive the fast, they recite the Buddha’s name; because they recite the Buddha’s name, they perfect the fast. Through this self-purification, they cause all people to have faith.
It is well to see that self-benefit is the foundation for benefiting others; thus, the gentleman seeks it within himself.
△ Second, mindfulness of the Dharma, in two parts: first, showing the object of mindfulness; second, clarifying the benefits of mindfulness. Now, the first part.
Second, one should mindfully contemplate the Dharma taught by the Buddha—the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—which are complete and unimpaired.
One should reflect upon them without forgetting, knowing that this Dharma is the illumination for the world.

Although the Buddha’s teachings are immeasurable, it is because these thirty-seven factors encompass the entire path of cultivation and realization from beginning to end that they alone [are emphasized].

When categorized, they are divided into seven groups: first, the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), which refer to the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena as the objects of observation;

second, the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), which mean that by means of the observation of the foundations of mindfulness, one prevents unarisen evil from arising, eliminates evil already arisen, brings about the arising of unarisen good, and increases good already arisen; third, the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), which refer to desire, mindfulness, [effort, and investigation].
Advancing wisdom within this context, one contemplates through meditative concentration; thus contemplating, one abandons [defilements] and is well able to accomplish the supernormal powers.

The four or five faculties (*indriya*) refer to faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, which constitute the untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*). The five powers (*bala*) are likewise named after the faculties;

that is, when faith and the others have increased, they are able to destroy the five hindrances. The seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) refer to mindfulness, the investigation of phenomena, and diligence.

With joy, lightness, tranquility, and equanimity, one disciplines the mind so that it neither sinks nor floats, thereby entering the Path of Seeing—the sevenfold and eightfold Noble Path consisting of right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right effort, right concentration, right mindfulness, and right livelihood.
One proceeds securely along this path through these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; the names and enumerations of these four categories are identical across all teachings.
Furthermore, as the contemplative wisdoms differ from one another, each possesses distinct variations in terms of vertical entry and horizontal integration;
because these can transport sentient beings of the three lands to the three types of nirvana, they constitute what the Threefold World clearly indicates must be fully possessed.
One should not neglect them, but rather maintain mindfulness without forgetting.
△ Second, explaining the benefits of mindfulness, in three parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the illustration by analogy; third, the application of the Dharma. Now, the first:

For one who mindfully contemplates the Dharma, ignorance, evil intentions, and the habit of anger are all eliminated, and a virtuous mind arises spontaneously, employing the practice of delighting in the Dharma.
The application of the four teachings to eliminate the four lands, the three poisons, and the residual habits of correct and false cultivation can be understood by analogy with what precedes.
△ Second, the illustration through metaphor:
It is like using sesame oil and cleansing powder to bathe away the filth and turbidity of the body.
When one observes the precepts, one takes the Dharma as the body; thus, the body is used as a metaphor for the Dharma.
This Dharmakāya is inherently pure by nature, yet it is illusorily formed by the defilements of the three delusions. Once these defilements are removed, the Dharmakāya is revealed.
△ III. The Threefold Convergence.
Regarding those who practice the mindfulness of the Dharma, their purity is such that all who see them cannot fail to feel faith and admiration.
△ III. Mindfulness of the Sangha. Part One: First, showing the object of mindfulness; second, clarifying the benefits of mindfulness. Now, the first [part].
Third, one should mindfully reflect upon the assembly of the Buddha’s disciples who are reverent, devoted, and rely upon his teachings.
Among them are those who have attained the stage of Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) and realized its fruit; those who have attained the stage of Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) and realized its fruit;

those who have attained the stage of Non-returner (anāgāmin) and realized its fruit; and those who have attained Arhatship (arhat) and realized its fruit. These constitute the four pairs and eight classes of noble beings.
Indeed, by perfecting the precepts, concentration, wisdom, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, and by accomplishing noble virtue and conduct,
one should join one's palms as a field of merit for the world of gods and men.

The Sanskrit term *saṃgha* is translated here as "harmonious assembly" (*hehezhong*). Now, when we simply say "assembly" (*zhong*), it is because the four pairs and eight ranks naturally possess both the harmony of principle and the harmony of phenomena.
The Vinaya explains that there are four kinds of assemblies: first, the "shameless assembly," referring to those who have broken the precepts;
second, the "dumb sheep assembly," referring to those who, though not having broken the precepts, are ignorant of the rules and the Dharma. Third...

The "pure Saṃgha" refers to the seven types of noble persons (saptakula-putra) both internal and external, as well as ordinary worldlings who maintain the precepts. The "true Saṃgha" refers to the four pairs and eight classes of noble ones (*catur-yugā aṣḍa-pudgalāḥ*).
Since one is now being instructed to recollect the true Saṃgha, it is said: "With reverence, one draws near and relies upon them to receive their wisdom and teaching.

"Reverence" pertains to the mind; "drawing near" pertains to the body; and "receiving the teaching" pertains to the speech. When the sixteen moments of mind are fulfilled, one first ascends [to the fruit].

The noble stage called "attaining the stream-entry" (srotāpanna) is also termed "entering the stream" (*gotrabhū*); this refers to the fruit of *srotāpanna*, wherein one is fully endowed with the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) but lacks one portion of the [eight] knowledges (*jñāna*).
One who is said to "realize entering the stream" is one who will inevitably realize the path of stream-entry without interval; this refers to the stage of *srotāpanna-pratipannaka*.
Having abandoned six categories of afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm, one is said to "attain the once-returner" (*sakṛdāgāmin*), which is also termed "coming back once."

Upon the first return, one who has abandoned five grades [of afflictions] is called a "recipient of the realization of the Once-returner" (sakṛdāgāmin), which is the stage of the candidate for the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka).

When the nine grades of thought-afflictions of the desire realm are completely exhausted, one is said to have attained the "Non-returner" (anāgāmin)—meaning "one who does not come back"—which is the fruit of non-returning;

at the point of abandoning the eighth grade, one is called a "recipient of the realization of the Non-returner," which is the stage of the candidate for the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmipratipannaka).

To exhaustively sever the delusions of the three realms is called attaining *arhatship* (the state of a Worthy One), because one is constantly in accord with the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). This refers to the fruit of Arhatship.

To further sever the afflictions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is called receiving the realization of *arhatship*; this refers to the stage of the candidate for Arhatship (*arhattva-pratipannaka*).

These two together constitute the "four pairs" and are divided into "eight classes. "Class" (*varga*) means a category. Because they are fully endowed with both wisdom and the abandonment [of defilements], they are so named.
The nature of the Great Man (puruṣa), which is characterized by the obstruction of impurity and the indestructible essence of non-action, is called the perfection of *śīla* (precept).

The attainment of the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), the nine successive attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), and so forth, is called the perfection of *samādhi* (concentration). The realization of the four noble truths is called the perfection of *prajñā* (wisdom).

The attainment of liberation from all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) is called the perfection of *vimukti* (liberation). [The text is missing the word for] the perfection of *vimuktijñānadarśana* (knowledge and vision of liberation); this is the analysis of the causes of liberation.
The non-erroneous nature of the fruit is called "crossing over"; the perfection of knowledge and vision is called "accomplishing wisdom.
Entering the stage of correctness is called "sagehood," and the fulfillment of virtuous conduct is called "perfection of practice. To state it in brief:
the first three fruits and the four stages of approach constitute the partial realization of the fivefold Dharma-body, while the fruit of Arhatship constitutes its full realization.
As for the body, one should join the palms in the *añjali* mudrā; by raising the joined palms, one gathers the three karmas.
As for the mind, one should contemplate the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) among the honored ones above and below heaven; by contemplating the field of merit, one manifests virtuous conduct.
Thus, when a lay bodhisattva receives the fast (*upavāsa*) and contemplates the assembly, they should certainly apply themselves with diligence in the three karmas toward the true Saṃgha.
One should likewise prostrate to and make offerings to pure monks; yet one must especially not treat with contempt or insult even those who are like "dumb sheep" or those lacking a sense of shame.

For if even the elephant king and the rākṣasa show reverence and submission to the *kāṣāya*—neither harming nor devouring it—how much more so should those who have taken refuge in the Triple Gem, who call themselves lay followers (*upāsaka*), and who practice as pure practitioners? The clear instructions of the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra* are manifest.
If one hesitates to strike a rat for fear of damaging a nearby vessel, this worldly maxim serves as a metaphor for which one should reflect with caution.

Furthermore, these four pairs and eight kinds [of practitioners] are explained here according to the *Āgama* teachings; however, in the Mahāyāna, although the contemplative wisdoms differ, there is no distinction in their severance and realization.

To distinguish between the Separate and the Perfect, one must rely on the dharmas of the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) and the five aggregates beyond the realms (*dhātu*) to discern the persons and phenomena. Thus, it should be known that... [the statement].

Although this is explained in terms of the Small Vehicle, its reality actually encompasses the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, regarding the Sangha Jewel as the contemplation of mind: this mind is fundamentally not form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental objects;
thus it is called a *srotāpanna*. This mind arises and perishes moment by moment; thus it is called a *sakṛdāgāmin*. When this mind has ceased and leaves no trace, it is called an *anāgāmin*.
When this mind does not arise through the four modes of existence (*catur-vidha-jāti*), it is called an *arhat*.

This nature of mind, being free from defilement, constitutes the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla*); this nature of mind, being unshakable, constitutes the perfection of meditative concentration (*samādhi*);

this nature of mind, being incapable of being obscured, constitutes the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā*). This nature of mind, not being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), is called the perfection of deliverance (*vimukti*);

this mind’s universal knowledge of all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena is called the perfection of the knowledge and vision of deliverance (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*). This is explained thus through the four teachings in succession.
Contemplation can be attained through the mind.
△ Second, clarifying the benefits of mindfulness, in three parts: first, the direct clarification; second, the illustration by analogy; third, the application of the Dharma. Now, for the first:
"This mindfulness completely eliminates the habits of the many ignorant, evil intentions, and anger; a heart of joy arises spontaneously, and one delights in the practice of the assembly."
A mind of joy is itself a virtuous mind; other cases may be understood by analogy with the preceding.
△ Second, the illustration by metaphor:
It is like using strong lye to wash clothes, whereby stains and impurities are removed.

The pure ash is also a metaphor for the four teachings; the Sangha Jewel of mindfulness and wisdom belongs to the virtue of liberation, and is therefore likened to clothing—namely, what is called the "garment of liberation.
It is also the adornment of shame and remorse, and the nature-inherent Sangha Jewel of the supreme patience of cessation.
Just as the body must have clothing, so too, when mindfulness and wisdom remove defilements, liberation is purified and all virtues are perfected.
He is adorned with gentleness and is well-disciplined and compliant.
△ Third, the correspondence of dharmas:
The virtue of one who maintains mindfulness of the assembly is such that all who see him will not fail to regard him with faith and admiration.

△ Fourth, mindfulness of precepts, in two parts: first, showing the objects of mindfulness; second, clarifying the benefits of mindfulness. Now, for the first part. "Four" refers to mindfulness of precepts:
receiving the Buddha’s precepts with the body and mind, upholding them with single-minded devotion, without deficiency or violation, without wavering or forgetting.
One establishes them well and guards them with care. For the sake of wisdom, one acts so as to have no cause for regret later. Without expectations, one is able to teach others equally.
The Buddha’s precepts differ according to the seven or nine assemblies and the two categories of Great and Small Vehicles.
When it is now said that one “receives the Buddha’s precepts,” this refers specifically to the eightfold precepts observed for a single day and night;

these eightfold precepts fully encompass the precepts of meditative concentration (*samādhi-saṃvara*), the precepts of the Path (*mārga-saṃvara*), as well as the three groups and five branches of precepts. Therefore, the general admonition says: “With a single mind.”
To uphold [the precepts] without deficiency or transgression is the *prātimokṣa* (liberation) vow; to be unshakable is the vow associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi-saṃvara*);

to be without forgetfulness is the vow associated with the Path (*mārga-saṃvara*). Furthermore, being without deficiency, without transgression, and unshakable constitutes the vow of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*);

being without forgetfulness, up to and including having no regrets in the future, constitutes the vow of gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*); and being without expectation while being able to teach others equally constitutes [the vow of benefiting sentient beings].
The precept of gathering sentient beings is also unimpaired, meaning that one protects and maintains the four root foundations without deficiency;

this is the precept of purity regarding the fundamental actions. It is unviolated, meaning that the remaining four branches as well as the outflows and preparatory means of the roots are entirely free from violation;
this is the precept of purity regarding the preceding and following attendants. It is immovable, meaning it is not shaken by desire.
When the realms are coarse and wretched, being moved by the five sensory objects, one does not engage in various evil thoughts but awakens to pure precepts;
this is called the presence of right mindfulness. Because of this, one is able to skillfully establish oneself and guard them with vigilance.
Even if one is questioned or examined by those possessed of wisdom, one can act as one speaks and speak as one acts; subsequently, having no cause for regret, this is protection.

To maintain right mindfulness and uphold the pure precepts without expectation—meaning not seeking for oneself the rewards of human or celestial fortune, nor the stages of the provisional vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—and to be able to teach others equally, saying:

"Relying solely upon the Supreme Vehicle, one should resolve to attain Bodhicitta and vow that all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm shall simultaneously attain unsurpassed Bodhi. This is...
Dedicating [the merit] toward the fulfillment of the unsurpassed path-precepts— taking these very one day and one night of the eightfold *upavāsa* precepts as the object of focus—
if within them one fulfills the three clusters and five branches associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the path (*mārga*), without deficiency or remainder,
then this constitutes the treasury of all the infinite merits of the Buddha-dharmas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; thus, the fast and precepts serve as...
In the Dharma-realm, all dharmas tend toward the precepts of fasting and restraint; there is no tendency beyond this, and this is what is called "mindfulness of the precepts.

If the observance of the fast for a single day and night—encompassing both the horizontal and vertical dimensions—is already like this, how much more so is it for the lifelong five precepts, the śrāmaṇera precepts, and the bhikṣu precepts?
Yet, the world holds the precepts and rules in contempt, seeking instead some other form of perfect and subtle realization.
This is truly inconceivable!
△ Second, clarifying the benefits of mindfulness, in three parts: first, the direct clarification; second, the illustration by analogy; third, the application to the Dharma. Now, for the first:

This practitioner who mindfully observes the precepts completely eliminates ignorance, evil intentions, and the habit of anger; a heart of joy arises spontaneously, and they take delight in the practice of the precepts.
The Three Jewels of Abiding exist by virtue of the precepts, and the Three Jewels of Unity are realized by virtue of the precepts;

thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that "fully upholding the dharma of the precepts of dignified conduct can cause the lineage of the Three Jewels to remain unbroken," which is why they are called the "unifying function."
△ Second, the illustration by analogy:
Just as a mirror, when its tarnish is removed through polishing, becomes filled with brilliant clarity;

so too, within the Three Jewels in their essential unity—wherein the Buddha is the head, the Dharma is the body, and the Sangha is the garment—it is only the precepts that can illuminate and reveal them.
Therefore, the *Prātimokṣa* states: "It is like a person looking into a mirror, where beauty or ugliness gives rise to joy or sorrow. It also says:
"The precepts are like a true jewel-mirror; they reflect all phenomena without exception.
△ Third, the correspondence with the Dharma.
The purity of one who recollects the precepts while observing the fast is like this; when others see them, there is none who does not respond with faith and admiration.
△ Fifth, Recollection of the Devas (1) First, showing the objects of recollection; (2) clarifying the benefits of recollection. Now, the first part.
Fifth, one should keep the heavens in mind: first, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings; second, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; the Yāma Heaven; the Tuṣita Heaven; the Nirmāṇarati Heaven;
and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. One should reflect upon their significance by considering that they possess faith, ethical discipline, learning, generosity, and wisdom.
The state of being naturally retributive and without deliberate effort is called "Heaven" (*deva*).
The Four Heavenly Kings—Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the East, Virūḍhaka in the South, Virūpākṣa in the West, and Vaiśravaṇa in the North—are those who protect the four continents;
they dwell on the terraces of Mount Sumeru at a distance of forty thousand *yojanas* from the earth. The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (the Heaven of the Thirty-three) translates here as "Thirty-three."
The Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa) resides on the summit of Mount Sumeru; in each of the four directions there are eight heavens, and among them, Śakra rules over the four continents.
It is eighty thousand *yojanas* above the earth. It is also called the Heaven of Flames (Yan-tian) and the Yāma Heaven.

This is translated as "Time-portion" (*kāla-bhāga*), meaning that while the light of the sun and moon shines upward but does not reach their bodies, they possess their own radiance, like lotus flowers.

Because its opening and closing constitute day and night, sixteen thousand *yojana*s above the earth, within the void of space, there is a ground that rests clearly like a cloud. This is the Tuṣita Heaven—also called Dōshutsu and Toshi;
this translates as "Contentment," meaning that one knows contentment regarding the five desires. It is thirty-two thousand *yojana*s above the earth.

Ten *yojana* above is the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati*), also called the Heaven of Emanated Pleasures; this means that they emanate various objects of pleasure according to their will, yet without indulgence or arrogance.
Sixty-four hundred thousand *yojana* above that is the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*), also called the Heaven of Sovereignty over Others' Emanations;
this means that the objects of pleasure they enjoy appear spontaneously and effortlessly without requiring deliberate mental effort. It is one hundred and twenty [thousand *yojana*] above that.
The eighty thousand *yojanas* do not refer to the form or formless realms;
rather, they are mentioned briefly in proximity because the merit of observing the fast for one day and night can induce the retributive fruits of these six heavens.
This is the fruit of mindfulness. Next, "I possess faith and so forth" refers to the causes of mindfulness, arising from faith in the Triple Gem and the precepts.
Because they uphold the precepts of the fast without violation, because they have heard this Dharma-gate of the Great Mantra,
because they are able to universally benefit sentient beings through their merit, and because they possess correct wisdom that is clear and free from inversion,

they are born among these six heavens to experience supreme and wondrous bliss, gradually attaining *nirvāṇa*. These six heavens are situated near the desire realm and are what people delight in hearing about.

First, the world universally hears that the fruits of the six heavens must be planted through virtuous causes; second, humans universally fear the gods, such that they dare not commit evil when under their gaze and hearing;
third, as an antidote, one comes to know the impermanence of the heavens and realizes the wisdom of suffering and the untainted true illumination;
fourth, regarding the ultimate truth, the principle of dependent origination within the six heavens belongs to the Tripitaka teachings.

The Heaven of Purity through Expedient Means (*upāya-śuddha-deva*) corresponds to the meaning of the "Single Phrase of Emptiness" in the Shared Teaching (*pāṭha-sādhāraṇa*); the Heaven of True Reward (*bhoga-vipāka*) corresponds to the meaning of "Successive Entry" in the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-bheda*);
the Heaven of Great Nirvāṇa of Tranquil Radiance (*śānta-prabhā-mahā-nirvāṇa*) corresponds to the meaning of "Immediate Identity with the Center" in the Perfect Teaching (*ekayāna*).

There are four [levels] regarding the faith in dharmas: the faith in the arising and ceasing of dharmas, the faith in the non-arising of dharmas, the faith in the immeasurability of dharmas, and the faith in the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*) nature of dharmas.

The four types of precepts taught by the teachings are: the precept of maintaining the nature, the precept of maintaining the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the precept of maintaining the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and the precept of maintaining the Middle Way.

The four types of hearing according to the teachings are: hearing the exposition of arising and ceasing, hearing the exposition of non-arising, hearing the exposition of the immeasurable, and hearing the exposition of the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

The four types of relinquishment according to the teachings are: relinquishing conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), relinquishing partial emptiness, relinquishing the attachment to the two extremes, and relinquishing [all attachments].
The Middle Way’s love consists of the four teachings; the wisdom of analytical dharma and the wisdom of the essence of dharma constitute the three wisdoms in succession.

The single mind possessing the three wisdoms constitutes the wisdom of the four teachings. For those who contemplate the mind: all worlds are established based upon the mind, hence it is named "Upholder of the Realm" (*Dhṛtarāṣṭra*);
all dharmas are produced from the mind, hence it is named "Increasing" (*Virūḍhaka*); the entire dharma-realm is one...
The mind seeing everywhere is named *Viśvadarśin* (Broad Vision); the single mind universally penetrating all dharma-gates is named *Bahusruta* (Much-Hearing);

the single mind fully possessing the merits of the King of Gods is named *Trāyastriṃśa* (Heaven of the Thirty-three); the single mind taking birth-and-death and nirvana as day and night is named *Yāma* (Salt Heaven);
not grasping at dharmas outside the mind is named *Tuṣita* (Joyous); and the single mind fully possessing the joy of the Dharma...

Heedfulness is called being free from arrogance and delighting in single-mindedness; transforming according to one’s will while not diminishing the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity is called the "transformative response to sound.
When one gives rise to faith within one's own mind and returns to trusting that very mind, it is called "having faith.
To be able to contemplate the nature of the mind and be fully endowed with the Buddha-dharma is called "having precepts."
To hear that one does not grasp at the dharmas of the three periods of time outside the mind is called having the knowledge of giving (*dāna*).

To know that the mind itself is empty, provisional, and the middle way is called having wisdom (*prajñā*). Furthermore, while many sutras clarify the "six remembrances" (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), this [text] subsumes them under the "remembrance of giving.

Moreover, regarding this dharma-gate of the "remembrance of deities," the Āgamas clarify the remembrance of the six heavens; that is, the remembrance of the ten [virtues] by which [one is reborn there].
Because they are wholesome, one is born in the heavens; yet these heavens are also suffering, empty, impermanent, and non-self—this is mostly the intent of the Tripitaka Teaching (Zangjiao).
The *Avataṃsaka* clarifies the mindfulness of the Great Being who is destined for birth in Tuṣita Heaven as a single-lifetime successor—this is mostly the intent of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao).
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* clarifies the mindfulness of the Heaven of the Ultimate Truth (Paramārtha)—this is mostly the intent of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). As for the matter in this present sutra:
Since these same Āgamas serve as the basis for all rational contemplation through their various causes, conditions, events, and contexts, how could one not seek them out with profound diligence?
△ Second, explaining the benefits of mindfulness, in three parts: first, the direct explanation; second, illustration by analogy; third, the application to the Dharma. Now, the first part.

For one who contemplates the heavens, ignorance, malevolence, and the habit of anger are all eliminated, and a joyful mind arises spontaneously; such a person delights in the sovereign work of the heavens.
The *Avataṃsaka* clarifies that the ten wholesome paths serve as the foundation for the five vehicles; thus, the karmic work of the heavens governs all.
△ Second, the illustration by analogy:
For example, a precious gem is constantly polished until it is clear and bright.
This is used to clarify the activity of the heavens through the adornment of merit; thus, like a precious gem, it is refined and polished in ten ways.

Thus, one is able to rain down jewels upon the four continents through the power of celestial karma; by repeatedly practicing mindfulness, one can assist the supramundane roots of goodness of the Three Vehicles.
△ Third, the correspondence of dharmas.
The purity of one who observes the fast while mindful of the heavens is thus.
△ Third, the conclusion of the three [sections]: first, the formal conclusion; second, manifesting its excellence; third, exhorting its observance. Now, the first:
To uphold the eight precepts and practice the five recollections constitutes the Buddhist fast.
△ Second, the manifestation of excellence:
sharing merit with the devas, extinguishing evil and promoting good, being reborn in the heavens, and ultimately attaining *nirvāṇa*.
"Sharing merit with the devas" refers to the world; "extinguishing evil" refers to the antidote; "promoting good" leads to rebirth as a human in heaven. *Nirvāṇa* is the ultimate goal.
The foremost meaning of the [Huan] River can be understood through the provisional teachings.
△ Third, the exhortation to uphold:
For this reason, the Wise One personally practices with vigor and creates merit from the depths of his heart.
Not falling into views of craving is called being wise; not relying on others is called practicing through one's own effort.
To have inner and outer as one is called giving rise to the mind to cultivate merit. If one does not practice with effort, it is the same as tending cattle;

if one does not give rise to this mind, it is to value the letter while disparaging the substance, which is the same as the Nirgranthas. May the wise examine this carefully. The section on the orthodox teaching is concluded.

△ Section Three: The Distribution for Circulation (Parīndanā), in two parts: First, the manifestation of the merit and retribution; Second, the faithful acceptance and practice. Within the first part, there are two sub-sections:
First, the manifestation of the superiority of the merit; Second, the demonstration of the excellence of the retribution. Now, the first [sub-section].
In this way, the merit, blessings, and illustrious reputation of the Vaiyāghrī fast extend far and wide;
even if the sixteen great kingdoms of the world were filled with immeasurable treasures, they would not equal the merit of observing the Buddhist Dharma fast for a single day.
To compare their merits, those sixteen kingdoms would be like a single bean.

This text is incomplete; it should state that the merit obtained from giving as an offering the sixteen realms filled with all manner of precious jewels does not equal the merit of observing the fast for a single day.

This is because the gift of rare treasures is merely a cause for happiness and pleasure in future lives, whereas the fast observed for one day and night is definitively a cause for transcending the world. Furthermore, as for rare treasures...
This is because it is the perfection of the gift of material wealth, the observance of precepts, the gift of Dharma, and the gift of fearlessness.

△ Second, showing the excellence of the retribution, which has two parts: first, presenting the characteristics of the fruit; second, clarifying the characteristics of the cause. Now, the first [part].
The vastness and distance of the heavens are beyond description. Fifty years in the human realm constitute one day and night in the first heaven;
the lifespan in that first of the four heavens is five hundred years, which corresponds to nine million years in the human realm.
Those who observe the Buddhist fast will be reborn in this heavenly realm.
The heavens above are vast and far-reaching, beyond all description; this serves as a general indication of the superior rewards of the six celestial realms.

First, the characteristics of the first heaven, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*), are presented, briefly citing the longevity of its inhabitants to manifest the abundance of their merit.

Other sutras clarify that one is born in this heaven by practicing the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*) in their highest degree. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* clarifies that it is through the merit of abstaining from killing that one attains birth there.
"O Deva, today you have clearly understood that by observing the Buddhist *poṣadha* one can be born in this heaven.
The ten wholesome paths (*daśakuśala*) constitute the true Dharma of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) in the world; non-killing is the lifelong precept of a partial *upāsaka*.
The Buddhist *poṣadha* is a day and a night of diligent merit, through which all may attain this retribution; yet the fruits of the *poṣadha* dharma do not stop here."
This is detailed as explained in the following text:

one hundred years among humans constitutes one day and night for the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; the lifespan of the Trāyastriṃśa devas is one thousand years, which corresponds to thirty-six million years by human reckoning.
Other sutras clarify that by cultivating the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*) to a superior degree, one attains birth in this heaven;

the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* clarifies that through the merit of refraining from killing and stealing, one attains birth in this heaven; now, it is further clarified that through the Buddhist fast (*upoṣadha*), one also attains birth there.
Two hundred human years constitute one day and night in the Salt Heaven; the lifespan in the Salt Heaven is two thousand years, which corresponds to one hundred fifty-two million human years.
Other sutras clarify that by practicing the ten wholesome actions of the highest grade (*uttama-pakṣa*) while also training in seated meditation, one attains birth in this heaven.
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* clarifies that through the merit of not killing, not stealing, and not engaging in sexual misconduct, one attains birth in this heaven.

Now, since one may also attain birth here through the methods of the fast (*upoṣadha*), it should be stated as "one hundred million plus forty-four million years. I suspect the translator was not proficient [in the calculation].
The numerical figures may be dialectal variations or perhaps errors in transcription.

Four hundred years among humans constitute one day and night in Tuṣita Heaven; the lifespan in Tuṣita Heaven is four thousand years, which corresponds to six hundred and eighty million years among humans.

Other sutras clarify that by practicing the ten wholesome actions of the highest grade (*uttama-kuśala-karma-patha*) while also engaging in seated meditation (*dhyāna*), one attains the "subtle abiding" (*sūkṣma-vihāra*) of the desire realm and is reborn in this heaven.
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* clarifies that through the merit of the three bodily and four verbal wholesome actions, one is reborn in this heaven;
here, it is also said that through the method of the fast (*upoṣadha*), one may be reborn there, and the lifespan should be stated as fifty million, seventy-six million years.
Eight hundred human years constitute one day and night for the gods of the Heaven of No-Contention (Atapa).
The lifespan of the gods of the Heaven of No-Contention is eight thousand such years, which corresponds to twenty-three billion four hundred million human years.

Other sutras clarify that one is born in this heaven by practicing the ten wholesome actions of the highest grade while concurrently cultivating the *anāgamya-samādhi* (the stage of access concentration);
according to the present method of observing the fast (*upavāsa*), one should likewise be said to be born there for twenty-three million, four hundred thousand years.
One thousand six hundred years among humans constitutes one day and night in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven;
the lifespan in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven is sixteen thousand years, which corresponds to nine billion two hundred and sixteen million years among humans.

Other sutras clarify that one is born in this heaven by practicing the ten wholesome actions of the highest grade while simultaneously attaining the concentration of the "not-yet-reached" stage (*anāgamya-samādhi*);
according to the present method of observing the fast (*upavāsa*), one should be said to be born there after ninety-two million times ten million plus one hundred and six million years.
△ Second, explaining the characteristics of the causes:

If a person possesses faith, precepts, learning, generosity, and wisdom, and observes the Buddhist fast, then at the time of their life’s end, their spirit will be reborn in these six heavens above, where they will dwell in peace, security, and happiness; their wholesome qualities will be many, while their faults will be few.
It is said that when ordinary people perform wholesome deeds, their spirits ascend to heaven to receive immeasurable blessings;
they rely upon lightness and ease. The remainder is as explained previously.

△ Second, the acceptance with faith and the practice of observance, which has two parts: first, the observance by those for whom the teaching is intended; second, the acceptance with faith by the great assembly. Now, the first part.
Upon hearing the Buddha’s words, Vīra was filled with joy and said, “Excellent, excellent, World-Honored One! The merit of the fast is most wonderful and immeasurable.
I pray that you will accept my observance of the precepts; from this day forward, on the six days of the fast each month, I shall exert all my strength to cultivate merit until death.”

The exhaustion of the life-span is called death; furthermore, the total severance of ignorance is called death. The former refers to the specific teaching [of this scripture], while the latter refers to the transition between stages.
△ Second, the great assembly’s faithful acceptance.
When the Buddha had finished preaching the sutra, they all received his instructions with joy.

Because the one who could preach was pure, they rejoiced; because he preached the Buddha-dharma to deliver sentient beings without ever harboring thoughts of fame or profit, the Dharma he taught was pure, and thus they rejoiced.
This is the true and essential gateway to transcending the world, which differs from the views of attachment and prejudice.

Because by discussing and hearing the Dharma one obtains supreme benefit; because one rejoices in present merit and happiness and is reborn in a good realm in future lives, ultimately attaining Great Nirvāṇa.
Thus ends the annotated commentary on the *Buddha-bhāṣita-upoṣadha-sūtra*.

Appendix: The Method for Receiving the Eight Precepts of the Uposatha (The various sūtras and śāstras all clarify the method for the eight precepts of the uposatha; generally speaking, while the five precepts serve as the cause for rebirth as a human or deva, it is the one-day and one-night fast that constitutes the cause for transcending the world.

This applies regardless of whether one has already received the five precepts or not, and even those who have received the bodhisattva or upāsaka precepts may receive and maintain them at will—whether on the six fasting days, their own birthdays, or the anniversaries of their parents' deaths—and should do so with a resolute mind).

(Although this sūtra combines [the precepts] into eight branches, there is no fault in reciting them as nine branches when receiving them; for while the phrasing may expand or contract, the meaning neither increases nor decreases. This is based on the *Vibhāṣā* and other texts to facilitate the formal declaration.)
I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha for one day and one night as a pure-practice upāsaka (or upāsikā).
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is my World-Honored One. (Recite this three times; if [the candidate] is unable, the preceptor should instruct them.

I, [Name], have completed taking refuge in the Buddha, have completed taking refuge in the Dharma, and have completed taking refuge in the Saṃgha for one day and one night as a pure-practice [upāsaka].
"Upāsaka (or Upāsikā), the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is my World-Honored One" (recite this three times; next, one should be taught the method for receiving the precepts).

"I now take the merit of these Eight Precepts and the Fast to universally repay the four debts of gratitude and provide sustenance for all beings within the three realms of existence, so that together with all sentient beings, we may be born in the Pure Land" (the first eight branches are called 'precepts,' and because abstaining from eating at improper times constitutes the 'fast,' they are termed the 'Eight Precepts and the Fast').

The *Sarvāstivāda-vibhāṣā* states: "When undertaking the eight precepts of the fast (*upavāsa*), one should say 'for one day and one night' regarding the abstention from killing, so as to ensure the language is definitive and not confused with lifelong precepts. The Buddha originally established that one day and one night is the limit which may not be exceeded;
if one has the capacity to receive them for one day, once that period has passed, one may receive them again in succession."

The extent of the practice depends on one's capacity and does not take the number of days into account. As for the method of receiving the *upavāsa* (fasting) precepts, one must necessarily receive them from others among the five assemblies (*pañca-saṃgha*).

The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states: "If someone has previously sent a messenger intending to execute another person, and the messenger has not yet arrived when that person subsequently resolves to receive the *upavāsa* precepts;
at the very moment they receive the precepts, the messenger arrives and immediately kills him."
Furthermore, at one time, because of the use of a ritual knife, one does not incur the sin of killing.

If those of noble rank constantly command others to commit evil, they must first issue a formal decree to cease such prior evils before they may receive the *zhāi* (fast/abstinence); only then will it be accomplished.
If one receives the *zhāi* without first ceasing [evil], it is not called attaining the *zhāi*. Those who wish to receive the *zhāi* should first proclaim their intention to all.
"Within the borders of my realm, I wish to observe the fast; on all days of fasting, I shall completely cease all evil deeds and acts of punishment and execution."
